title: Greedy Best-First in Lisbon: Fast, but risky!
description: Watch Greedy Best-First sprint across real street-like nodes, always choosing the next step that looks closest to the goal. It’s quick, but can get trapped—perfect for visualizing informed graph search behavior.
ig_caption:
🚦 Lisbon’s waterfront grid is a perfect playground for **Greedy Best-First**! 🌊

In this visualization, we model the streets as a **graph**: intersections become **nodes**, road segments become **edges**, and each step picks the neighbor with the smallest **heuristic h(n)** (typically straight-line distance). 🧠⚡

That “greedy” choice means Greedy Best-First is **informed** but not guaranteed to be optimal—so you’ll see paths that look promising locally while sometimes missing a globally shortest route. 📉🗺️

🔍 Mechanic: at every expansion, the frontier prioritizes the node with minimum **h(n)** (no need to track cumulative cost like Dijkstra). This makes it feel lightning-fast, but it’s more vulnerable to misleading heuristics.

yt_description:
Greedy Best-First pathfinding visualization in Lisbon (Parque das Nações)! 🗺️⚡

In this YouTube Shorts video, we convert street-like locations into a graph (nodes + edges) and run **Greedy Best-First search** using a heuristic (e.g., straight-line distance to the goal). You’ll see how the algorithm makes fast, locally informed expansions—why it can look “smart” yet still miss the true shortest route.

Keywords: greedy best-first, pathfinding, graph search, shortest path, heuristic, algorithms, coding visualization, AI navigation, computer science.
